opus-5.5.text:
For me, it comes down to a few signals, and honestly most of them are the same ones we watched for in the early days of Transformers.

The first is whether people are actually *building* things, not just starring the repo. Are they recording datasets with their own robots and pushing them to the Hub? Are they training policies on those datasets and sharing the checkpoints? When I see someone in a garage somewhere with a low-cost arm, collecting fifty episodes of folding a towel and uploading them, that's a much stronger signal than any download count. It means the barrier to entry is low enough that the long tail of people can participate.

The second is diversity: of hardware, of tasks, of places in the world. Robotics has historically been very concentrated in a few well-funded labs with very expensive hardware. If LeRobot only ends up being used by those same labs, then we haven't really changed anything. So I look at the variety of embodiments showing up, at the hackathons happening in cities we never organized anything in, at students contributing drivers for robots we've never heard of.

The third is whether the community starts surprising us. In the Transformers days, the moment I knew it was working was when people started using the library for things we never imagined. Same here. When someone takes a policy, fine-tunes it on a totally different task, and it kind of works, or finds a better way to do data collection than we did, that tells me the community has its own momentum and isn't just following our roadmap.

And then, more quietly, I watch the quality of the data. Robotics is going to be bottlenecked by data for a while, so if the shared datasets get bigger, cleaner, and better standardized over time, that compounding is really what will matter in the long run. It's less flashy than a cool demo video, but it's the foundation everything else stands on.

r001.rationale: The response says shared datasets should get bigger over time and mentions people uploading datasets to the Hub, but it does not identify exponential growth in the number of LeRobot datasets there.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't judge it by the benchmarks. The benchmarks in robotics are still so immature that if you optimize for them, you can fool yourself very quickly. What I look at is much more mundane: are people actually building things, and are they sharing them?

The thing that convinced me we were on the right track was when the community started to surprise me. In the beginning, it was mostly us at Hugging Face pushing datasets and policies, and the community was consuming. At some point that flipped. People started showing up with their own robot arms, their own datasets recorded in their living rooms, their own training scripts, and sometimes they were ahead of us. That's the signal. Open source works when the center of gravity moves away from the people who started it.

The second thing I look at is the cost curve. If the only people who can participate are labs with a couple of hundred thousand dollars of hardware, then it's not really a community, it's a club. So when I see someone fine-tune a policy on a robot that cost a few hundred dollars, and it does something that actually works, I pay more attention to that than to a flashy demo from a well-funded team. Because that's the thing that scales. That's what happened with language models, right? The moment people could run and fine-tune models on their own machine, the whole field accelerated.

And then there is the honest part, which is the failures. A healthy community talks about what doesn't work. Robotics has a long tradition of cherry-picked videos, and I think we are all a bit allergic to that now. When I see people posting the twenty failed attempts alongside the one that worked, and other people jumping in to debug it, I think, okay, this is real research happening in public, not a marketing channel.

So I would say: diversity of contributors, low cost of entry, and honesty about what's hard. If those three keep going in the right direction, I'm not too worried about any specific number on a leaderboard. The numbers will follow.

r001.rationale: The response cites diverse contributors, affordable participation, and openness about failures as signals. It does not identify exponential growth in the number of LeRobot datasets on the Hub.

astra-6.text:
I think the real test is whether people can build on each other’s work. Can someone take a robot, use a dataset or a model that somebody else shared, and get it doing something useful without starting from scratch? And can they then contribute what they learned back to the community?

If that loop is working—if it’s getting easier for new people to join, reproduce results, and improve them—then I’d say the community is on the right track. A great demo is exciting, but seeing other people reproduce it and take it somewhere you didn’t expect is a much stronger signal.

r001.rationale: The response points to people sharing, reproducing, and building on work, but does not identify exponential growth in the number of LeRobot datasets on the Hub.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the strongest signal is whether people can build on each other’s work. Can someone collect a dataset, share it, and then have someone else use it to train a robot or improve a policy? If every project requires starting from scratch, we’re missing something.

So I’d look beyond the number of people following the project. Are people contributing their own experiments? Are they sharing failures as well as successes? Are newcomers able to reproduce results and then try something different? If that loop is working, the community is on the right track.

r001.rationale: The response discusses sharing and reusing datasets, but it does not identify exponential growth in the number of LeRobot datasets on the Hub as evidence of progress.
